initial_question: What can observed accuracy establish when a forecast is made public to an agent able to respond to it?
initial_claim_disposition: The broad observation that publicly disseminated predictions can change predicted outcomes is established in the checked sources. Do not present it as novel.

closest_existing_argument.author: Kenneth Stalkfleet
closest_existing_argument.coverage: Full ten-page article read, especially pp. 75-78.
closest_existing_argument.relevance: Gene's stock forecast is justified and self-fulfilling; Stalkfleet considers a no-prophecy counterfactual repair to the causal theory of knowledge.
closest_existing_argument.limit: The proposed repair is examined, not adopted as a universal account of knowledge.

strongest_rival.authors: Owen C. King and Mayli Mertens
strongest_rival.work: Self-fulfilling Prophecy in Practical and Automated Prediction
strongest_rival.coverage: Selected sections of full 26-page PDF; see source note.
strongest_rival.relevance: Their taxonomy already separates transformative from operative causal contribution and self-securing cases; they explain how accuracy can hide process mistakes and make counterfactual classification difficult.

other_close_sources: Matthew Kopec (2011), probabilistic reflexivity and the variable evidential force of observed outcomes.
Mayli Mertens et al. (2022), hidden false positives and poor learning from self-fulfilling neuroprognoses; excerpt only.
Juan C. Perdomo et al. (2020), deployed prediction changes the outcome distribution and is evaluated under the induced distribution.
Michael P. Kim and Juan C. Perdomo (2023), accuracy and steering are different decision objectives under outcome performativity.
Donal Khosrowi (2023), model performativity is contextual and both actual and counterfactual forecasts matter.
provisional_contribution: A modest proposition-indexing diagnosis: distinguish a forecast of the choice under the disclosed-forecast policy (Y^1) from a forecast of the choice under non-disclosure (Y^0). Accuracy about Y^1 does not establish truth or knowledge about Y^0; a causal contribution to Y^1 alone does not defeat knowledge of Y^1.
scope: Binary choice in a one-shot setting with a forecast generated before the choice and an explicit disclosure regime.
The essay evaluates what observed exposed-regime accuracy supports; it does not offer a general theory of knowledge, agency, free will, forecasting, or causal inference.
The thesis is an inferential limitation, not a blanket claim that self-fulfilling forecasts cannot be knowledge.
Computational results, if any, concern only the specified finite structural-model class.
defeaters: The distinction merely repeats established potential-outcomes or reflexive-prediction terminology without a useful epistemic consequence.
The claim wrongly treats Y^0 and Y^1 as the same proposition or misstates Stalkfleet's candidate repair.
A forecast that reliably predicts a known response policy already provides knowledge of exactly the proposition at issue; then the argument only blocks an inference to a different target.
The finite model search demonstrates only generic observational non-identifiability and adds no philosophical insight.
originality_limit: The checked primary sources are targeted rather than exhaustive. No claim that no prior author has made this proposition-indexing point is warranted.
